cognate: Ved. sána- = Gk ἕνος (*sénos 'old'); Ved. náva-/návya- = Gk νέος (*néwos 'new'); both members cognate
drift_or_renewal: none in the adjectives; the Greek binomial is frozen as a calendar term (ἕνη καὶ νέα 'old-and-new day', last day of the lunar month), in which ἕνος survives almost only here
shared_syntax: coordinated adjective pair 'old and new' (Ved. sánā návā ca, Gk ἕνη τε καὶ νέα), substantivised; in RV 1.174.8 the two are set against each other in one clause (the old [deeds] have come as new)
context: Polar merism 'old and new' made of the two inherited adjectives. In the Veda it totalises Indra's deeds (old and new) or the waters/plants; in Greek it names the day where the old moon ends and the new begins, and Plato glosses it as the moon's light that is 'always new and old'. The Greek use is a fixed archaic binomial preserved in legal/calendar language, which is the kind of fossil an inherited pair leaves; the Vedic sánā návā ca is the same coordinated pair. Generic merism type, but the material is cognate on both sides and the Greek member ἕνος is otherwise nearly lost, so the binomial predates Greek. recalled: Lith. sẽnas ir naũjas as a further match; not checked in a local corpus

cognate: Gk γλυκύς/γλυκερός = Lat. dulcis (*dl̥kú-, a Graeco-Latin isogloss); Gk μέλι = Lat. mel (*mélit)
shared_syntax: epithet + noun 'sweet honey' (Hom. μέλιτι γλυκερῷ ~ Lat. melle dulci) and the comparative of the epithet with honey as standard (Hom. μέλιτος γλυκίων ~ Plaut. melle dulci dulcior); Il. 1.249 and Thesm. 1192 tie the sweetness to the tongue/speech
context: Honey as the standard of sweetness, applied to speech or a beloved: Nestor's voice 'sweeter than honey' from his tongue (Il. 1.249), the Scythian's 'sweet tongue like Attic honey' (Thesm. 1192), Plautus' 'sweeter than sweet honey' to a lover, Lucretius' 'sweet honey of the Muses' for verse. Same cognate epithet with the same cognate noun and the same comparative figure in both languages. Low: 'honey is sweet' is near-universal, and Plautus (Greek models) and Lucretius (Greek honeyed-cup image) may be imitating Greek rather than continuing an inherited phrase. Recalled: Hitt. maliddu- 'sweet' derived from milit 'honey' shows the association but not this pairing.

cognate: Gk λύκος = ON ulfr (*wĺ̥kʷos); Gk κέχηνα (χάσκω/χαίνω) and ON gína belong to one 'gape' root complex (*ǵʰeh₂-/*ǵʰyeh₂-), but are different formations
shared_syntax: noun + participle of 'gape' agreeing with it: λύκῳ κεχηνότι ~ Ulfr gínandi
context: 'Gaping wolf' as an image of menace: in Aristophanes the Spartans are as trustworthy as a gaping wolf (proverbial); in Hyndluljóð it is a warrior's byname in a genealogy list. Germanic myth also has the gaping wolf Fenrir (recalled). The contexts are not congruent (simile vs nickname), and a wolf gaping is an obvious image, so this is a weak lead only.

note: Mostly Hippocratic and Cato prose pivots with partners sharing common roots (numerals, body parts, wine, seasons); nothing inherited there. Three claims: old-and-new merism (medium), sweet honey (low), gaping wolf (low). Rejected: waking/sleeping (B-0444e, B-7609e, B-f9197: Hippocratic prose against Vedic jā́grato/svápantaḥ, sleep verb renewed, no shared context); ON fegri þykkir ~ OE fægere þūhton (B-b7a2a, same branch).
